feedback: When signals disagree (two point to eruption, one doesn't), prompt the learner to say how that lowers certainty rather than forcing a yes/no.
After a false alarm, reinforce that acting on strong converging evidence can be correct even when no eruption follows.
After a missed sign, discuss what extra monitoring or cross-checking might catch it next time, and why perfect prediction isn't possible.
activities.intendedInsight: Experiencing signals that rise together, conflict, or surprise you is intended to show that risk judgement draws on converging evidence and that uncertainty is built in, not a flaw.
learnerActions: Watch a set of gauges - gas level, ground tilt/deformation, and earthquake (seismicity) activity - change over a scenario.
Decide whether to raise or lower an alert level (e.g. green -> amber -> red) as the signals rise together or disagree.
Play through outcomes that include a false alarm and a missed sign, and read feedback framed as 'good decision under the evidence available', not simply right/wrong.
Explain afterwards which signals drove your call and how confident you could reasonably be.
activities.title: Make the call: an observatory monitoring panel

feedback: For the 'certain' distractor, re-explain that a red alert issued before an eruption expresses a judged high risk from combined evidence, not a guarantee of an eruption.
For a correct match, restate the underlying mechanism briefly to reinforce understanding over rote recall.
activities.intendedInsight: A quick recognition check can confirm learners hold the key facts and the crucial distinction that a high alert issued before an eruption means high judged risk, not certainty.
learnerActions: Match each warning sign to what it can indicate (rising gas emissions / ground swelling / earthquake swarms -> possibly magma moving up, though each can have other causes).

Answer selected-response questions such as 'In this activity's alert scale, what does a red alert issued before any eruption mean?', choosing 'the risk is judged high from the combined evidence' and rejecting the tempting distractor 'an eruption is certain'. (In some real alert systems, red can also be used once an eruption is already happening.)
activities.title: Check understanding: signs, causes and what an alert means
